overview.purpose: slop is a file concatenation format that bundles multiple source files into a single markdown file for transmission to AI systems. Your role is to deserialize (deslop) these files, perform requested tasks, and reserialize (reslop) the results.
workflow: Receive a slopified markdown file containing multiple source files
Parse the slop block headers to reconstruct the original files
Create the original files in your working environment
Perform the requested tasks (analysis, modifications, debugging, etc.)
Reslop the modified files back into a single slop file (*.slop.md)
Return the slop file so the user can deslop to get edited files

slop_format_specification.description: A slop file is a markdown file containing concatenated source files, each preceded by a slop block header.

slop_marker.description: Required marker identifying the start of a slop block

file_path.description: The original file's path, double-quoted and properly escaped
notes: Path separators use forward slashes (/) even on Windows
Special characters in paths are escaped as needed
Relative or absolute paths should be preserved as provided

sloped_lines.description: The exact number of lines in the file content that follows

trailing_newline.description: Boolean indicating whether the original file ended with a newline character
notes: This is crucial for exact file restoration
Each file's content follows immediately after its slop block header
Content spans exactly the number of lines specified in #SLOPED_LINES
Multiple slop blocks are concatenated sequentially in the slop file
No extra separators between slop blocks—next header follows immediately

deslop.description: Convert a slop file back into the original files
algorithm: 1. Open and read the entire slop file
2. Scan for lines matching the pattern: #SLOP "<path>" #SLOPED_LINES <N> #SLOP_TRAILING_NEWLINE <bool>
a. Extract the file path from the quoted string
b. Extract the line count (N) to know how many lines follow
c. Extract the trailing newline boolean
d. Read exactly N lines after the header into a buffer
e. Create parent directories for the file path as needed
f. Write the buffer to disk at the specified path
g. If trailing_newline is false, remove the final newline from the file
4. Repeat until all slop blocks are processed
implementation_notes: Handle path escaping: unescape any escape sequences in the path
Track line numbers carefully to extract exactly N lines
Create parent directories if they don't exist (mkdir -p equivalent)
Preserve file permissions and metadata from the original path if possible
Handle edge cases: empty files (N=0), files with no trailing newline

reslop.description: Convert modified files back into a slop file
algorithm: 1. Identify all files you've modified or created during your work
a. Read the complete file content into memory
b. Count the total number of lines (split on newline, accounting for the final state)
c. Determine if the file ends with a newline character
d. Generate the slop block header: #SLOP "<path>" #SLOPED_LINES <count> #SLOP_TRAILING_NEWLINE <bool>
e. Append the header followed by the exact file content to the slop output
3. Write all concatenated slop blocks to a new file with a .slop.md extension
implementation_notes: Line count should match exactly what will be written
To count lines: split content by \n, but be careful with the final newline
- If content is "line1\nline2" (no trailing newline): line_count = 2, trailing=false
Escape special characters in file paths as needed for the slop format
Include all modified files, not just changed ones (in case deletions/renames matter)

malformed_headers.description: If a header doesn't match the expected format, treat it as a parsing error
malformed_headers.recovery: Report the line number and problematic content to the user

missing_metadata.description: If a slop block header is missing #SLOPED_LINES or #SLOP_TRAILING_NEWLINE
missing_metadata.recovery: Report what metadata is missing and which file path was partially parsed

line_count_mismatch.description: If fewer lines exist after a header than #SLOPED_LINES specifies
line_count_mismatch.recovery: Report the expected line count vs. actual lines found, and the affected file path

best_practices: Always validate slop block headers before consuming file content
Track your file modifications carefully so you can reslop accurately
When desloping, create parent directories automatically
Preserve the exact line count when resloping—off-by-one errors will corrupt the slop file
Handle the trailing newline flag correctly; it's essential for exact file restoration
For files with no content, use #SLOPED_LINES 0 and #SLOP_TRAILING_NEWLINE false
If the user requests specific files to return, only reslop those files
Document any files you create or modify that aren't in the original slop—add them to the reslopified output
